topics.name: Brown v. Board of Education
topics.kicker: Unanimous 1954 Supreme Court ruling · Struck down school segregation
topics.briefing: Linda Brown was a third grader in Topeka, Kansas, who had to travel across town to an all-Black school even though a school for white children was much closer to her home. Her father, Oliver Brown, joined an NAACP lawsuit, and lawyer Thurgood Marshall carried the fight to the Supreme Court. On May 17, 1954, Chief Justice Earl Warren read the unanimous ruling: “separate educational facilities are inherently unequal.”
topics.answerHtml: Brown v. Board of Education of Topeka (prompt on Brown alone or on school desegregation; do not accept “Plessy v. Ferguson”)
accept: brown v board of education of topeka
brown v board of education of topeka kansas
brown v the board of education
brown v topeka board of education

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Psychologists Kenneth and Mamie Clark found that many Black children preferred white dolls to Black dolls, and this decision cited their research in its eleventh footnote. This decision declared that separating children by race “generates a feeling of inferiority” that may affect their “hearts and minds.”
tossups.r: Chief Justice Earl Warren wrote it. For 10 points, name this 1954 Supreme Court case that struck down segregation in public schools.

tossups.p: In 1951, sixteen-year-old Barbara Johns led a student strike against crowded, run-down conditions at Robert Russa Moton High School in Farmville, Virginia. The lawsuit that grew out of that strike was one of the cases the Supreme Court combined under this case’s name.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1954 case in which NAACP lawyer Thurgood Marshall persuaded the Court to end school segregation.

tossups.p: John W. Davis, a former Democratic nominee for president, argued for South Carolina in _Briggs v. Elliott_, a case from Clarendon County that the Supreme Court combined with this one. Lawyers on the other side argued that segregation itself, not just unequal buildings, violated the Constitution.
tossups.r: This case was named for a father in Topeka, Kansas. For 10 points, name this 1954 case that overturned “separate but equal” in public schools.

tossups.p: Because Washington, D.C., is not a state, the Supreme Court decided its school case, _Bolling v. Sharpe_, under the Fifth Amendment on the same day as this case. This case itself relied on the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this unanimous 1954 decision that ended legal segregation in America’s public schools.

tossups.p: After Chief Justice Fred Vinson died in 1953, this case was argued a second time before his replacement, a former governor of California. That new Chief Justice worked to get all nine justices to agree, believing a unanimous ruling would be harder to resist.
tossups.r: That man, Earl Warren, read this ruling aloud in May 1954. For 10 points, name this case that struck down school segregation.

tossups.p: A year after this decision, a follow-up ruling ordered schools to desegregate “with all deliberate speed,” a vague phrase that many Southern districts used to delay for years. In 1956, about 100 Southern members of Congress signed the Southern Manifesto opposing this decision.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1954 Supreme Court case that overturned _Plessy v. Ferguson_ in public education.

tossups.p: Virginia senator Harry Byrd called for “massive resistance” to this decision, and Prince Edward County, Virginia, closed all of its public schools from 1959 to 1964 rather than obey it. In 1957, Arkansas governor Orval Faubus used the National Guard to keep nine Black students out of Little Rock’s Central High School.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1954 Supreme Court ruling that ordered an end to segregated public schools.

tossups.p: Earlier NAACP victories in _Sweatt v. Painter_, about a law school in Texas, and _McLaurin v. Oklahoma State Regents_ helped prepare the way for this case. The NAACP’s campaign that led to this case was planned by Charles Hamilton Houston, who trained a generation of Black lawyers at Howard University.
tossups.r: Houston’s former student Thurgood Marshall argued this case. For 10 points, name this 1954 case that struck down school segregation.

tossups.p: A third grader was turned away from the all-white Sumner Elementary School, which was much closer to her home, and had to attend the all-Black Monroe Elementary School instead. The Monroe school building later became a national park site honoring this case.
tossups.r: The lawsuit was named for her father, who lived in Topeka, Kansas. For 10 points, name this 1954 Supreme Court case that struck down school segregation.

tossups.p: This decision called education “perhaps the most important function of state and local governments” and concluded that separate schools are “inherently unequal.” It rejected the reasoning of an 1896 case that had upheld segregated railroad cars in Louisiana.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1954 case that ended the “separate but equal” rule in public schools.

tossups.p: In _Cooper v. Aaron_ (1958), all nine justices signed an opinion saying Arkansas officials could not ignore this earlier ruling. That case followed a 1957 crisis in which President Dwight Eisenhower sent the 101st Airborne Division to protect nine Black students in Little Rock.
tossups.r: This earlier case was argued by Thurgood Marshall. For 10 points, name this unanimous 1954 case that declared segregated public schools unconstitutional.

tossups.p: Norman Rockwell’s painting _The Problem We All Live With_ shows six-year-old Ruby Bridges walking between federal marshals to integrate a New Orleans elementary school in 1960. Bridges had been born in 1954, the same year this ruling came down.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Supreme Court case in which Earl Warren’s Court declared school segregation unconstitutional.

tossups.p: Seven years before this ruling, a federal appeals court decided _Mendez v. Westminster_, which ended the segregation of Mexican American students in parts of Orange County, California. The California governor who then signed a law ending school segregation in his state later wrote this ruling.
tossups.r: That man was Earl Warren. For 10 points, name this 1954 Supreme Court case that struck down laws requiring segregated public schools.

tossups.p: This decision called the history of the Fourteenth Amendment “inconclusive” on whether its writers meant to ban segregated schools, so it focused on the role of education in modern life. The Court had asked lawyers to research that history before the case was argued again in 1953.
tossups.r: Chief Justice Earl Warren wrote its opinion. For 10 points, name this unanimous 1954 school desegregation case.

tossups.p: Many people saw this decision as proof that Justice John Marshall Harlan had been right when he wrote, as the lone dissenter in an 1896 case, that “Our Constitution is color-blind.” This decision came 58 years after that case.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1954 case, argued by Thurgood Marshall, that overturned “separate but equal” in public schools.

trap.title: Plessy or Brown?
trap.body: Both cases are about “separate but equal,” so they show up together in many tossups. _Plessy v. Ferguson_ (1896) upheld segregated railroad cars in Louisiana and created that rule; _Brown v. Board_ (1954) struck it down for public schools. Some tossups ask for school desegregation itself, with clues like the Little Rock Nine and Ruby Bridges, and a 1955 follow-up ruling, often called “Brown II,” ordered desegregation “with all deliberate speed.”
trap.fix: Listen for the date and the verb: 1896, Homer Plessy, railroad cars, and “upheld” mean _Plessy_; 1954, Topeka, Earl Warren, and “struck down” or “overturned” mean Brown. If the question asks for “this process,” answer school desegregation; for “this case,” say the full name, because “Brown” alone only earns a prompt.
trap.line: Real answer line: Brown v. Board of Education of Topeka (prompt on Brown alone or on school desegregation; do not accept “Plessy v. Ferguson”)

topics.name: Chicago
topics.kicker: Illinois’s largest city, on Lake Michigan · Rebuilt after the fire of 1871
topics.briefing: Chicago began as a trading post where a small river meets Lake Michigan, and its name comes from a Native American word for a wild onion that grew there. Railroads, stockyards, and factories made it one of the fastest-growing cities in history. After the Great Chicago Fire of 1871 destroyed much of it, the city rebuilt with some of the world’s first skyscrapers.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: A trader of African descent, Jean Baptiste Point du Sable, is often called this city’s founder because he built a farm and trading post here in the 1780s. The U.S. Army built Fort Dearborn at this spot in 1803, but the fort was destroyed during the War of 1812.
tossups.r: This city later became the nation’s biggest railroad hub. For 10 points, name this city on Lake Michigan, the largest in Illinois.

tossups.p: In 1900, engineers opened the Sanitary and Ship Canal, which reversed the flow of this city’s river to carry sewage away from the lake that supplies its drinking water. That river is dyed green each year for Saint Patrick’s Day.
tossups.r: The Illinois and Michigan Canal, finished in 1848, had earlier linked this city to the Mississippi River system. For 10 points, name this largest city in Illinois.

tossups.p: Upton Sinclair’s novel _The Jungle_ follows Jurgis Rudkus, a Lithuanian immigrant who works in the meatpacking plants near this city’s Union Stock Yards. A Carl Sandburg poem calls this city the “Hog Butcher for the World” and the “City of the Big Shoulders.”
tossups.r: This city on Lake Michigan is nicknamed the “Windy City.” For 10 points, name this largest city in Illinois.

tossups.p: In 1886, a bomb exploded as police moved to break up a labor rally in this city’s Haymarket Square, where workers had gathered to support an eight-hour workday. Eight anarchists were convicted after that event, which is remembered each May Day around the world.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this city where, according to legend, Mrs. O’Leary’s cow started a great fire in 1871.

tossups.p: At a meeting held during a world’s fair in this city, Frederick Jackson Turner presented his “frontier thesis,” arguing that the frontier had shaped American democracy. That 1893 fair, nicknamed the “White City,” introduced George Ferris’s giant wheel.
tossups.r: That fair was the World’s Columbian Exposition. For 10 points, name this Illinois city on Lake Michigan.

tossups.p: In 1889, Jane Addams and Ellen Gates Starr opened Hull House, a settlement house that offered classes, child care, and other help to immigrant families in this city. Addams later became the first American woman to win the Nobel Peace Prize.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Illinois city where the gangster Al Capone made a fortune during Prohibition.

tossups.p: William Le Baron Jenney’s Home Insurance Building, finished in this city in 1885, is often called the first skyscraper because a metal frame, not thick stone walls, held up its weight. Louis Sullivan, who wrote that “form ever follows function,” also designed tall buildings here.
tossups.r: This city’s Sears Tower was the world’s tallest building from 1973 to 1998. For 10 points, name this city.

tossups.p: Robert Abbott’s weekly newspaper, the _Defender_, urged Black Southerners to move north to this city during the Great Migration, and many settled in its Bronzeville neighborhood. Muddy Waters and other musicians who moved here helped create an electric style of blues named for this city.
tossups.r: This city’s baseball teams are the Cubs and the White Sox. For 10 points, name this largest city in Illinois.

tossups.p: Abraham Lincoln won the Republican nomination for president in 1860 at a convention hall in this city called the Wigwam. Thirty-six years later, William Jennings Bryan gave his “Cross of Gold” speech at a convention here.
tossups.r: Its nicknames include the “Windy City.” For 10 points, name this largest city in Illinois.

tossups.p: Mayor Richard J. Daley led this city from 1955 until his death in 1976, and his son Richard M. Daley later served as its mayor for 22 years. In 1968, police clashed with antiwar protesters outside the Democratic National Convention in this city.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Illinois city whose O’Hare Airport is named for a World War II pilot.

tossups.p: On December 2, 1942, Enrico Fermi’s team achieved the first self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction under the stands of Stagg Field, at a university in this city. In 1983, Harold Washington became this city’s first African American mayor.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this city where the Sears Tower, later renamed the Willis Tower, was built.

tossups.p: Eight players on this city’s American League baseball team were banned from the sport for life after being accused of losing the 1919 World Series on purpose. Those players, including “Shoeless” Joe Jackson, were nicknamed the “Black Sox.”
tossups.r: This city’s National League team, the Cubs, plays at Wrigley Field. For 10 points, name this city.

tossups.p: Cyrus McCormick moved his factory for mechanical reapers to this city in 1847, and Aaron Montgomery Ward started one of the first mail-order catalog businesses here in 1872. Sears, Roebuck and Company also ran its famous catalog business from this city.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this railroad hub on Lake Michigan, the largest city in Illinois.

tossups.p: This city was incorporated as a town in 1833 and as a city in 1837, and its name comes from a Native American word for a wild onion or garlic plant that grew along its river. Its downtown business district is called the Loop.
tossups.r: Much of this city burned in a great fire in 1871. For 10 points, name this city on the southwestern shore of Lake Michigan.

tossups.p: Daniel Burnham, who led the building of the 1893 world’s fair, later co-wrote a 1909 plan for this city calling for a chain of public parks along its lakefront. This city’s Art Institute owns Grant Wood’s _American Gothic_ and Edward Hopper’s _Nighthawks_.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Illinois city, the third-largest U.S. city in the 2020 census.

clues.t: Largest city in Illinois, on the southwestern shore of Lake Michigan
A great fire in 1871, blamed in legend on Mrs. O’Leary’s cow, destroyed much of it
Nicknamed the “Windy City” and the “Second City”
Prohibition gangster Al Capone’s bootlegging gang was based here; he was convicted of tax evasion in 1931
Its Sears Tower (renamed the Willis Tower in 2009) was the world’s tallest building from 1973 to 1998
Home of baseball’s Cubs, who play at Wrigley Field, and White Sox
Its name comes from a Native American word for a wild onion or garlic plant
Hosted the World’s Columbian Exposition (1893), the “White City,” which introduced the Ferris wheel
Haymarket Affair (1886): a bomb exploded at a labor rally for the eight-hour workday
The Pullman Strike (1894) began in George Pullman’s company town on the city’s South Side
Upton Sinclair’s _The Jungle_ (1906) exposed its meatpacking plants near the Union Stock Yards
Jane Addams and Ellen Gates Starr founded Hull House, a settlement house for immigrants, in 1889
Carl Sandburg’s poem calls it “Hog Butcher for the World” and “City of the Big Shoulders”
Lincoln was nominated at the Wigwam (1860); William Jennings Bryan gave the “Cross of Gold” speech here (1896)
O’Hare International Airport is named for World War II Navy pilot Butch O’Hare
Jean Baptiste Point du Sable, a trader of African descent, was its first permanent non-Native settler (1780s)
Fort Dearborn (1803) was destroyed in the War of 1812; incorporated as a town in 1833 and a city in 1837
The Illinois and Michigan Canal (1848) linked it to the Mississippi; in 1900 the Sanitary and Ship Canal reversed its river’s flow
William Le Baron Jenney’s Home Insurance Building (1885), often called the first skyscraper; Louis Sullivan: “form ever follows function”
At a meeting during the 1893 fair, Frederick Jackson Turner presented his “frontier thesis”; Daniel Burnham led the fair’s building
Robert Abbott’s _Defender_ newspaper drew Black Southerners here in the Great Migration; many settled in Bronzeville, and Muddy Waters helped create its electric blues
Enrico Fermi’s team made the first self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction under the stands of Stagg Field (December 2, 1942)
Mayors Richard J. Daley (1955–1976) and his son Richard M. Daley (1989–2011); protests outside the 1968 Democratic convention
Harold Washington became its first African American mayor in 1983
Black Sox Scandal: eight White Sox players were banned after being accused of losing the 1919 World Series on purpose
Cyrus McCormick’s reaper factory (1847); Montgomery Ward (1872) and Sears, Roebuck mail-order catalogs
Daniel Burnham’s 1909 plan called for public parks along its lakefront; its Art Institute owns _American Gothic_ and _Nighthawks_

trap.title: City or event?
trap.body: Several separate answer lines are packed with clues about this city: the Great Chicago Fire (1871), the Haymarket Affair (1886), the Pullman Strike (1894), and the gangster Al Capone. A tossup that asks for “this fire,” “this strike,” or “this gangster” wants one of those, not the city. Also, Chicago is not the capital of Illinois; Springfield is.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun: “this city” wants Chicago. Mrs. O’Leary’s cow, Haymarket Square, George Pullman, and Al Capone can all show up inside a Chicago tossup, so if you are unsure what is being asked, wait for the last line.

topics.name: Democratic Party
topics.kicker: Oldest active U.S. political party · Party of Jackson, FDR, and the donkey
topics.dates: Formed in the late 1820s around Andrew Jackson
topics.briefing: The Democratic Party grew out of the supporters of Andrew Jackson in the late 1820s, which makes it one of the oldest political parties in the world that is still active. Its donkey symbol began as an insult to Jackson, and cartoonist Thomas Nast made it famous. Its presidents have ranged from Jackson and Grover Cleveland to Franklin Roosevelt, John F. Kennedy, and Barack Obama.
topics.answerHtml: Democratic Party (accept Democrats; do not accept “Democratic-Republican Party” or “Republican Party”)
accept: democratic party of the united states

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1835, a radical New York faction of this party got the nickname “Locofocos” after its members lit candles with friction matches when their opponents turned off the gas lights at a meeting. That faction opposed monopolies and the paper money issued by state banks.
tossups.r: This party grew out of Andrew Jackson’s supporters. For 10 points, name this party whose symbol is a donkey.

tossups.p: From 1832 until 1936, this party required its presidential nominees to win the votes of two-thirds of its convention delegates, a rule that forced a record 103 ballots at its 1924 convention in Madison Square Garden.
tossups.r: That convention finally chose John W. Davis. For 10 points, name this party that later nominated Franklin Roosevelt four times.

tossups.p: Antislavery members of this party in New York, nicknamed “Barnburners,” left it in 1848 to support Martin Van Buren as the Free Soil Party’s candidate for president. Their rivals within this party were called “Hunkers.”
tossups.r: Van Buren had won the presidency in 1836 as this party’s nominee. For 10 points, name this party founded by supporters of Andrew Jackson.

tossups.p: This party created its national committee in 1848. In June 1972, burglars were arrested inside that committee’s headquarters in Washington’s Watergate office complex, beginning a scandal that led Richard Nixon to resign.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this political party whose symbol, the donkey, was popularized by the cartoonist Thomas Nast.

tossups.p: At its 1860 convention in Charleston, South Carolina, this party split over slavery, and its Northern and Southern wings later nominated two different candidates, Stephen Douglas and John C. Breckinridge. That split helped Abraham Lincoln win the presidency.
tossups.r: Its first president had been Andrew Jackson. For 10 points, name this party, the main rival of Lincoln’s Republicans.

tossups.p: During the Civil War, opponents nicknamed members of this party who wanted an immediate peace with the Confederacy “Copperheads,” after a venomous snake. In 1864, this party nominated George McClellan, a general whom Abraham Lincoln had removed from command.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this party that opposed Lincoln’s Republicans and whose symbol is a donkey.

tossups.p: Thomas Nast’s cartoons in _Harper’s Weekly_ helped make animals the symbols of both this party and its main rival in the 1870s. Nast also attacked William “Boss” Tweed, whose Tammany Hall political machine controlled this party in New York City.
tossups.r: This party’s donkey symbol dates back to opponents calling Andrew Jackson a “jackass.” For 10 points, name this party.

tossups.p: Al Smith, a governor of New York who rose through the Tammany Hall political machine, became this party’s first Catholic nominee for president in 1928. He lost that election in a landslide to Herbert Hoover.
tossups.r: Thirty-two years later, this party’s nominee, John F. Kennedy, became the first Catholic president. For 10 points, name this party.

tossups.p: In 1932, Franklin Roosevelt flew to this party’s convention in Chicago and became the first major-party nominee to accept in person, promising “a new deal for the American people.”
tossups.r: His New Deal coalition kept this party in the White House until 1953. For 10 points, name this party.

tossups.p: In 1948, some Southern delegates walked out of this party’s convention after it adopted a civil rights plank backed by Minneapolis mayor Hubert Humphrey. Those Southerners then formed a States’ Rights party, nicknamed the “Dixiecrats,” behind Strom Thurmond.
tossups.r: This party’s nominee, Harry Truman, won the election anyway. For 10 points, name this party.

tossups.p: At this party’s 1964 convention in Atlantic City, Fannie Lou Hamer told a televised committee hearing about the dangers Black Mississippians faced when they tried to register to vote. Her group was challenging Mississippi’s all-white delegation.
tossups.r: That year, this party’s president, Lyndon Johnson, won a landslide victory. For 10 points, name this party.

tossups.p: After this party’s 1968 convention in Chicago, the McGovern–Fraser Commission changed its rules so that voters in primaries and caucuses, not party leaders, chose most delegates. In 1982, it added “superdelegates,” party officials free to support any candidate.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this party whose presidential nominees have included Jimmy Carter and Barack Obama.

tossups.p: At this party’s 1844 convention, James K. Polk became the first “dark horse” presidential nominee after former president Martin Van Buren, who opposed annexing Texas, failed to win two-thirds of the delegates.
tossups.r: Polk then won the election. For 10 points, name this party founded by supporters of Andrew Jackson.

tossups.p: Grover Cleveland was the first member of this party elected president after the Civil War, winning in 1884 and again in 1892. Four years later, this party nominated William Jennings Bryan, who called for the free coinage of silver.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this party that later nominated Woodrow Wilson and Franklin Roosevelt.

tossups.p: Since about the 2000 election, television networks have colored states won by this party blue. In 1984, it nominated Geraldine Ferraro, the first woman to run for vice president on a major party’s ticket.
tossups.r: In 2008, this party nominated Barack Obama, who became the first African American president. For 10 points, name this party whose symbol is a donkey.

trap.title: Three parties, one word
trap.body: Thomas Jefferson and James Madison’s party of the 1790s is usually called the Democratic-Republican Party. The modern Democrats grew out of one wing of it in the 1820s, but it is a separate answer line. The modern Republican Party is a different party, founded in 1854 by opponents of the spread of slavery, so answering “Republicans” is wrong too.
trap.fix: Use the date. Clues from the 1790s to the 1820s (Jefferson, Madison, James Monroe, rivalry with the Federalists) want the Democratic-Republicans. Clues from Jackson onward (the donkey, Van Buren, Bryan, FDR, blue states) want the Democratic Party. Lincoln, the elephant, and 1854 want the Republicans.
trap.line: Real answer line: Democratic Party (accept Democrats; do not accept “Democratic-Republican Party” or “Republican Party”)

topics.name: Federal Bureau of Investigation
topics.kicker: Federal crime-fighting agency founded in 1908 · J. Edgar Hoover’s G-men
topics.briefing: In 1908, Attorney General Charles Bonaparte, a grandnephew of Napoleon, created a small force of special agents to investigate federal crimes. Under J. Edgar Hoover, who ran it for 48 years, it became the FBI, famous for its “G-men,” its crime lab, and its Ten Most Wanted list. It also hunts spies and works to stop terrorism, and its new agents train at Quantico, Virginia.
topics.answerHtml: Federal Bureau of Investigation (accept FBI; accept Bureau of Investigation for the years before 1935)
reject: bureau of alcohol tobacco firearms and explosives

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: This agency was founded in 1908 by Attorney General Charles Bonaparte, a grandnephew of the French emperor Napoleon. Bonaparte created his own force of special agents after Congress barred the Justice Department from borrowing detectives from the Secret Service.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this federal law enforcement agency later led for 48 years by J. Edgar Hoover.

tossups.p: Congress gave this agency’s special agents general power to carry guns and make arrests only in 1934, during a wave of gangster crimes. Two years earlier, the kidnapping of aviator Charles Lindbergh’s baby son led to a law that let this agency pursue kidnappers across state lines.
tossups.r: Its agents were nicknamed “G-men,” short for “government men.” For 10 points, name this agency of the Justice Department.

tossups.p: In 1924, this agency began building a national collection of fingerprint records, and in 1932 it opened a crime laboratory to study evidence such as bullets and handwriting. Starting in 1935, it trained local police leaders in such methods at its National Academy.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Justice Department agency led from 1924 until 1972 by J. Edgar Hoover.

tossups.p: Since 1930, this agency has gathered crime statistics from police departments across the country in its Uniform Crime Reports. Its motto, “Fidelity, Bravery, Integrity,” uses words that begin with the same letters as this agency’s initials.
tossups.r: This agency publishes a Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list. For 10 points, name this federal law enforcement agency.

tossups.p: As head of the Justice Department’s General Intelligence Division, a young lawyer helped organize the Palmer Raids against suspected radicals in 1919 and 1920. In 1924, that lawyer took charge of this agency.
tossups.r: He led it until his death in 1972. For 10 points, name this agency run for decades by J. Edgar Hoover.

tossups.p: Agent Melvin Purvis led a team from this agency that tracked down the bank robber John Dillinger outside Chicago’s Biograph Theater in 1934. The Justice Department had called Dillinger “Public Enemy Number One.”
tossups.r: This agency’s agents were nicknamed “G-men.” For 10 points, name this federal agency led by J. Edgar Hoover.

tossups.p: In 1971, activists broke into this agency’s office in Media, Pennsylvania, and leaked files that exposed COINTELPRO, a secret program that spied on and tried to disrupt political groups. That program had targeted Martin Luther King Jr.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this agency led from 1924 to 1972 by J. Edgar Hoover.

tossups.p: In 2005, Mark Felt, who had been the second-ranking official of this agency, revealed that he was “Deep Throat,” the secret source who helped two _Washington Post_ reporters uncover the Watergate scandal.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this agency that J. Edgar Hoover had led until his death in 1972.

tossups.p: After a senator criticized him for never having arrested anyone himself, this agency’s director went to New Orleans to take part in the arrest of the gangster Alvin Karpis in 1936. Karpis had been a leader of the Barker gang.
tossups.r: That director was J. Edgar Hoover. For 10 points, name this federal law enforcement agency.

tossups.p: After its longtime director died in office in 1972, Congress limited later directors of this agency to a single ten-year term. That longtime director’s name was given to this agency’s headquarters building on Pennsylvania Avenue in Washington, D.C.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this agency led for 48 years by J. Edgar Hoover.

tossups.p: New special agents of this agency train at an academy on a Marine Corps base in Quantico, Virginia. According to a popular story, its agents got a famous nickname in 1933 when George “Machine Gun” Kelly shouted, “Don’t shoot, G-men!”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this federal agency that publishes a Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list.

tossups.p: In 1942, this agency arrested eight German saboteurs who had landed from submarines on Long Island and in Florida, after one of them turned himself in. In 1950, it arrested Julius Rosenberg on charges of spying for the Soviet Union.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this federal agency whose longtime director was J. Edgar Hoover.

tossups.p: After the September 11 attacks in 2001, this agency made preventing terrorism its top priority, working with local police through Joint Terrorism Task Forces. Earlier, during the Cold War, it hunted Soviet spies inside the United States.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this federal law enforcement agency in the Department of Justice, once led by J. Edgar Hoover.

tossups.p: A 1949 news story about the “toughest guys” this agency wanted to catch inspired a list that it began publishing in March 1950. Many fugitives on that list have been caught after members of the public recognized their photos.
tossups.r: That list is called the “Ten Most Wanted Fugitives.” For 10 points, name this agency.

tossups.p: In 1908, some members of Congress opposed creating this agency because they feared it would become a federal secret police. President Theodore Roosevelt supported his attorney general, who set it up anyway while Congress was out of session.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this agency, which took its full modern name in 1935 under J. Edgar Hoover.

trap.title: Which federal agency?
trap.body: Several agencies get mixed up. This one investigates federal crimes inside the United States and is part of the Justice Department. The Central Intelligence Agency (1947) gathers intelligence overseas, and the Secret Service, created in 1865 to fight counterfeit money, protects the president. Eliot Ness’s “Untouchables,” who went after Al Capone, worked for the Prohibition Bureau, not this agency.
trap.fix: Federal crimes and spies inside the U.S., J. Edgar Hoover, G-men, and the Ten Most Wanted list mean the FBI. Spying overseas means the CIA; guarding the president or fighting counterfeiters means the Secret Service. If the question says “this man,” the answer is J. Edgar Hoover.
trap.line: Real answer line: Federal Bureau of Investigation (accept FBI; accept Bureau of Investigation for the years before 1935)

topics.name: First Amendment
topics.kicker: Five freedoms: religion, speech, press, assembly, petition · Ratified 1791
topics.briefing: The First Amendment packs five freedoms into one sentence: religion, speech, the press, peaceful assembly, and petitioning the government. James Madison wrote it as part of the Bill of Rights, ratified in 1791, and its opening words, “Congress shall make no law,” at first limited only the federal government. Supreme Court cases about flag salutes, school prayer, student armbands, and secret government papers have shaped what it means.
topics.answerHtml: First Amendment (or Amendment I; prompt on freedom of speech, freedom of religion, or freedom of the press; do not accept “Bill of Rights” or “Second Amendment”)
accept: first amendment to the united states constitution
first amendment to the us constitution
first amendment of the bill of rights
first amendment in the bill of rights
first amendment to the bill of rights

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: When Congress sent twelve proposed amendments to the states in 1789, this one was third on the list, but it took a lower number after the two proposals ahead of it failed to win ratification. One of those failed proposals was finally ratified in 1992 as the Twenty-seventh Amendment.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this part of the Bill of Rights that protects freedom of speech, religion, and the press.

tossups.p: In _Everson v. Board of Education_ (1947), Justice Hugo Black applied part of this amendment to the states and quoted Thomas Jefferson’s 1802 letter to the Danbury Baptists. In that letter, Jefferson said this amendment built “a wall of separation between church and state.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this amendment whose establishment clause bars Congress from setting up an official religion.

tossups.p: Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr. wrote that this amendment would not protect a man “falsely shouting fire in a theatre and causing a panic.” In that 1919 case about leaflets opposing the military draft, Holmes created the “clear and present danger” test.
tossups.r: That case was _Schenck v. United States_. For 10 points, name this amendment that protects freedom of speech.

tossups.p: In 1965, Iowa students Mary Beth Tinker, her brother John, and Christopher Eckhardt were suspended for wearing black armbands to school to protest the Vietnam War. In 1969, the Supreme Court ruled that their armbands were protected symbolic speech under this amendment.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this amendment, whose rights the Court said students do not shed “at the schoolhouse gate.”

tossups.p: A Montgomery, Alabama, city commissioner sued _The New York Times_ over an advertisement supporting Martin Luther King Jr., leading to a 1964 ruling that public officials must prove “actual malice” to win a libel case.
tossups.r: That case strengthened the freedom of the press protected by this amendment. For 10 points, name this amendment.

tossups.p: In 1971, the Supreme Court allowed newspapers to keep printing the Pentagon Papers, a secret history of the Vietnam War leaked by Daniel Ellsberg, ruling that the government had not justified stopping them. Forty years earlier, _Near v. Minnesota_ had also struck down a “prior restraint” on the press.
tossups.r: Both cases relied on this amendment’s protection of a free press. For 10 points, name this amendment.

tossups.p: On Flag Day in 1943, the Supreme Court ruled that public schools could not force Jehovah’s Witness students to salute the flag, overruling a decision from just three years earlier. Justice Robert Jackson wrote that no official can “prescribe what shall be orthodox in politics, nationalism, religion, or other matters of opinion.”
tossups.r: That case was _West Virginia State Board of Education v. Barnette_. For 10 points, name this amendment that protects freedom of speech and religion.

tossups.p: In _Engel v. Vitale_ (1962), the Supreme Court ruled that public schools could not lead students in a prayer written by New York state officials. A year later, it struck down required Bible readings in public schools in _Abington School District v. Schempp_.
tossups.r: Both rulings relied on this amendment’s establishment clause. For 10 points, name this amendment.

tossups.p: In _Texas v. Johnson_ (1989), the Supreme Court ruled 5–4 that burning an American flag as a political protest was symbolic speech protected by this amendment. Congress then passed the Flag Protection Act, which the Court struck down the next year.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this amendment that protects freedom of speech and of the press.

tossups.p: In _Brandenburg v. Ohio_ (1969), the Supreme Court ruled that speech can be punished only if it is meant to provoke “imminent lawless action” and is likely to do so. Decades earlier, _Gitlow v. New York_ (1925) began applying this amendment’s protection of speech to state governments.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this amendment that protects freedom of speech, religion, the press, assembly, and petition.

tossups.p: The 1735 trial of printer John Peter Zenger is seen as an early step toward this amendment’s protection of a free press. Less than seven years after this amendment was ratified, the Sedition Act of 1798 made it a crime to publish “false, scandalous and malicious” writing against the government.
tossups.r: Thomas Jefferson later pardoned people convicted under that law. For 10 points, name this amendment that guarantees freedom of the press.

tossups.p: In _Wisconsin v. Yoder_ (1972), the Supreme Court ruled that Amish parents could not be forced to keep their children in school after the eighth grade. In 1993, the Court sided with a Santería congregation in Hialeah, Florida, under the same part of this amendment.
tossups.r: That part is called the free exercise clause. For 10 points, name this amendment that protects freedom of religion.

tossups.p: In _Hazelwood School District v. Kuhlmeier_ (1988), the Supreme Court ruled that a Missouri principal could remove articles from a student newspaper written in a journalism class. That decision said schools may limit what students publish in school-sponsored papers for teaching reasons.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this amendment that protects freedom of the press, speech, and religion.

tossups.p: Under the 1833 case _Barron v. Baltimore_, rights like those in this amendment were held to limit only the federal government, not the states. In the 1900s, the Supreme Court applied this amendment’s protections to the states through the Fourteenth Amendment’s Due Process Clause.
tossups.r: This amendment begins “Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion.” For 10 points, name it.

tossups.p: For decades, courts used a three-part test from _Lemon v. Kurtzman_ (1971) to decide cases under this amendment’s establishment clause. In 2022, the Supreme Court ruled 6–3 for a high school football coach who prayed on the field after games and said it had abandoned that test.
tossups.r: That 2022 case was _Kennedy v. Bremerton School District_. For 10 points, name this amendment that protects freedom of religion.

Part of the Bill of Rights, ratified December 15, 1791
Begins “Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion”
Its religion clauses are the establishment clause (no official religion) and the free exercise clause
Thomas Jefferson’s 1802 letter to the Danbury Baptists said it built “a wall of separation between church and state”
_Tinker v. Des Moines_ (1969): students’ black armbands protesting the Vietnam War were protected speech
_Schenck v. United States_ (1919): Holmes’s “clear and present danger” test and “falsely shouting fire in a theatre”

_Engel v. Vitale_ (1962): public schools may not lead students in an official prayer
_Texas v. Johnson_ (1989): burning a flag in protest is protected symbolic speech
_New York Times Co. v. Sullivan_ (1964): public officials must prove “actual malice” to win libel suits
James Madison drafted it along with the rest of the Bill of Rights
Third of the twelve amendments Congress proposed in 1789; the two ahead of it failed, and one of them became the 27th Amendment in 1992
_Barron v. Baltimore_ (1833) limited the Bill of Rights to the federal government; _Gitlow v. New York_ (1925) began applying speech rights to the states (incorporation)
_Near v. Minnesota_ (1931): struck down a state “gag law,” limiting “prior restraint” of the press
_West Virginia v. Barnette_ (1943): schools may not force Jehovah’s Witness students to salute the flag; overruled _Gobitis_ (1940)

_Abington School District v. Schempp_ (1963): no required Bible readings in public schools

_Lemon v. Kurtzman_ (1971) created a three-part test; in _Kennedy v. Bremerton_ (2022), the Court ruled 6–3 for a coach who prayed after games and said it had abandoned that test
_Wisconsin v. Yoder_ (1972): Amish parents may keep their children out of school after eighth grade
_Hazelwood v. Kuhlmeier_ (1988): schools may limit what students publish in school-sponsored newspapers

trap.title: Amendment or freedom?
trap.body: This amendment is one part of the Bill of Rights, so “Bill of Rights” is wrong when a question asks for one amendment. Some tossups ask for just one of its freedoms, such as “freedom of the press,” and want that exact answer instead. Its neighbors are easy to mix up too: the Second Amendment protects the right to keep and bear arms, and the Fifth lets people refuse to testify against themselves (“pleading the Fifth”).
trap.fix: Listen for the noun. “This amendment” wants “First Amendment”; “this right” or “this freedom” wants the specific freedom. School prayer, the wall of separation, black armbands, flag burning, and the Pentagon Papers are all First Amendment clues.
trap.line: Real answer line: First Amendment (or Amendment I; prompt on freedom of speech, freedom of religion, or freedom of the press; do not accept “Bill of Rights” or “Second Amendment”)

topics.name: Second Amendment
topics.kicker: Protects the right to keep and bear arms · Ratified 1791
topics.briefing: The Second Amendment is a single 27-word sentence: “A well regulated Militia, being necessary to the security of a free State, the right of the people to keep and bear Arms, shall not be infringed.” Ratified in 1791 as part of the Bill of Rights, it has been read in different ways, and in 2008 the Supreme Court ruled in _District of Columbia v. Heller_ that it protects an individual’s right to keep a handgun at home for self-defense.
topics.answerHtml: Second Amendment (or Amendment II; prompt on right to bear arms; do not accept “Bill of Rights,” “First Amendment,” or “guns”)
accept: second amendment to the united states constitution
second amendment to the us constitution
second amendment of the bill of rights
second amendment in the bill of rights
second amendment to the bill of rights
prompt: right to keep and bear arms

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: George Mason’s Virginia Declaration of Rights of 1776 called “a well regulated militia, composed of the body of the people” the “proper, natural, and safe defence of a free state.” This amendment also drew on the English Bill of Rights of 1689, which let Protestant subjects have arms for their defense.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this amendment that protects “the right of the people to keep and bear Arms.”

tossups.p: James Madison’s 1789 draft of this amendment would have excused anyone “religiously scrupulous of bearing arms” from being forced to serve in the military, but the Senate cut that clause. Many supporters of this amendment feared that a permanent national army could threaten liberty.
tossups.r: This amendment comes right after the one protecting free speech. For 10 points, name this amendment protecting the right to keep and bear arms.

tossups.p: The year after this amendment was ratified, the Militia Act of 1792 required able-bodied white male citizens between the ages of 18 and 45 to enroll in their state’s militia and supply their own musket or rifle. Anti-Federalists had worried that the Constitution gave Congress too much power over the state militias.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this amendment that begins “A well regulated Militia, being necessary to the security of a free State.”

tossups.p: In _United States v. Cruikshank_ (1876) and _Presser v. Illinois_ (1886), the Supreme Court said this amendment limited only the federal government, not the states. That changed in 2010, when the Court applied it to state and local governments.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this amendment that protects the right to keep and bear arms.

tossups.p: In _United States v. Miller_ (1939), the Supreme Court upheld a federal tax and registration law covering short-barreled shotguns, saying there was no evidence that such a weapon was connected to a “well regulated Militia.” That law, the National Firearms Act of 1934, also regulated machine guns.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this amendment, which protects “the right of the people to keep and bear Arms.”

tossups.p: Dick Heller, a special police officer who carried a handgun while guarding a federal building, sued after Washington, D.C., refused to let him keep a handgun in his home. In 2008, the Supreme Court ruled 5–4 that the city’s handgun ban violated this amendment.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this amendment that protects the right to keep and bear arms.

tossups.p: Justice Antonin Scalia’s majority opinion in a 2008 case divided this amendment into a “prefatory clause” about the militia and an “operative clause” that protects an individual right. Justice John Paul Stevens’s dissent argued that the right was tied to service in a state militia.
tossups.r: That case was _District of Columbia v. Heller_. For 10 points, name this amendment about the right to keep and bear arms.

tossups.p: A 2008 ruling on this amendment called the handgun “the quintessential self-defense weapon” but said long-standing limits, like bans on carrying guns in schools and government buildings, could remain. In 2016, in a case about a stun gun, the Court said this amendment’s protection is not limited to weapons that existed in the 1700s.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this amendment, which protects “the right of the people to keep and bear Arms.”

tossups.p: Justice Samuel Alito wrote the main opinion in a 2010 case that applied this amendment to state and local governments through the Fourteenth Amendment. Justice Clarence Thomas agreed with the result but relied instead on the Fourteenth Amendment’s Privileges or Immunities Clause.
tossups.r: That case was _McDonald v. City of Chicago_. For 10 points, name this amendment protecting the right to keep and bear arms.

tossups.p: In a 2022 case, Justice Clarence Thomas wrote that gun laws must be consistent with “this Nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulation.” That case struck down New York’s rule that people show “proper cause” to get a license to carry a handgun in public.
tossups.r: That case was _New York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen_. For 10 points, name this amendment.

tossups.p: In _United States v. Rahimi_ (2024), the Supreme Court voted 8–1 to uphold a federal law that bars people under certain court protective orders from having guns. Chief Justice John Roberts’s opinion clarified a historical test that the Court had announced two years earlier.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this amendment that protects the right to keep and bear arms.

tossups.p: For many years, legal scholars debated whether this amendment protects a “collective right” connected to service in state militias or an “individual right” of each person to own guns. A 2008 Supreme Court decision adopted the individual-right reading.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this amendment, whose text begins by mentioning “A well regulated Militia.”

tossups.p: Colonial militias, such as the Massachusetts minutemen who turned out when British troops marched toward Concord in 1775, are often cited as background for this amendment. Its first clause says that a militia is “necessary to the security of a free State.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this amendment that also protects “the right of the people to keep and bear Arms.”

tossups.p: This amendment is a single sentence of just 27 words, ending with the phrase “shall not be infringed.” Its unusual commas and its opening clause about the militia have been debated by courts and scholars for many years.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this amendment, ratified in 1791, that protects the right to keep and bear arms.

tossups.p: In _Federalist_ No. 46, James Madison wrote of “the advantage of being armed, which the Americans possess over the people of almost every other nation.” The next year, Madison proposed this amendment to the First Congress.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this amendment that protects the right to keep and bear arms.

trap.title: Amendment, right, or weapons?
trap.body: This amendment is one part of the Bill of Rights, so “Bill of Rights” is wrong when a question asks for one amendment. Some tossups ask for the weapons themselves, with answer lines like “guns” or “firearms”; a question about how weapons were invented or made, such as Samuel Colt’s revolver or the Springfield Armory, wants that kind of answer instead. On either side of this amendment sit the First (speech, religion, and the press) and the Third (no quartering of soldiers in private homes).
trap.fix: Listen for the noun. “This amendment” wants “Second Amendment”; “these weapons” or “these objects” wants guns or firearms; “this document” wants the Bill of Rights. If you hear “keep and bear Arms,” “well regulated Militia,” _Heller_, or _McDonald_, say “Second Amendment.”

topics.name: Joseph McCarthy
topics.kicker: Wisconsin senator of the Red Scare · Gave his name to McCarthyism
topics.briefing: In 1950, a little-known Wisconsin senator named Joseph McCarthy claimed that he had a list of communists working in the State Department. For four years he made headlines with accusations he often could not prove, and his name became a word: McCarthyism. In 1954, televised hearings about the Army and a broadcast by journalist Edward R. Murrow hurt his popularity, and the Senate voted to condemn him.
topics.answerHtml: Joseph McCarthy (accept Joe McCarthy; do not accept “Eugene McCarthy”)
reject: house committee on un american activities

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Senator Margaret Chase Smith of Maine and six other Republican senators issued a “Declaration of Conscience” in 1950 criticizing this man’s tactics, though Smith never mentioned him by name. Months earlier, this man had claimed in Wheeling, West Virginia, to have a list of communists working in the State Department.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Wisconsin senator whose name became a word for accusing people of disloyalty without proof.

tossups.p: A Senate subcommittee led by Millard Tydings of Maryland called this man’s charges against the State Department “a fraud and a hoax,” and this man then campaigned against Tydings, who lost his reelection race in 1950.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Wisconsin Republican who led a hunt for communists in the federal government in the early 1950s.

tossups.p: In 1946, this Wisconsin circuit judge upset Senator Robert La Follette Jr. in a Republican primary, campaigning as “Tail Gunner Joe” based on his service in the Marine Corps during World War II.
tossups.r: He later chaired a Senate subcommittee that investigated suspected communists. For 10 points, name this senator from Wisconsin.

tossups.p: In a long 1951 Senate speech, this man accused former Secretary of State George Marshall of taking part in a vast conspiracy, and Dwight Eisenhower later dropped a passage praising Marshall from a 1952 campaign speech in this man’s home state.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this senator from Wisconsin who led an anticommunist campaign in the early 1950s.

tossups.p: This man’s chief counsel, Roy Cohn, was accused of seeking special treatment for G. David Schine, a former consultant to this man’s subcommittee who had been drafted into the Army. Those charges led to weeks of nationally televised hearings in 1954.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Wisconsin senator, a leading figure of the Second Red Scare in the early 1950s.

tossups.p: During a 1954 hearing, this man said that Fred Fisher, a young lawyer at Joseph Welch’s Boston law firm, had once belonged to the National Lawyers Guild. Welch then asked him, “Have you no sense of decency, sir, at long last?”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Wisconsin senator who was censured by the Senate later that year.

tossups.p: Edward R. Murrow devoted a 1954 episode of his CBS program _See It Now_ to criticizing this man, mostly by showing clips of this man’s own speeches. A 2005 film about that broadcast took its title from Murrow’s sign-off, “Good night, and good luck.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Wisconsin senator who made sweeping charges of communist influence in the government.

tossups.p: Senator Ralph Flanders of Vermont introduced a resolution against this man, and a special committee led by Arthur Watkins of Utah recommended that the Senate condemn him. In December 1954, the Senate voted 67 to 22 to condemn his conduct.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Wisconsin Republican who led a campaign against suspected communists.

tossups.p: _Washington Post_ cartoonist Herbert Block, known as Herblock, is often credited with coining a word from this man’s name in a 1950 cartoon. That word came to mean attacking people’s loyalty without solid evidence.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this senator who claimed in 1950 that communists were working in the State Department.

tossups.p: A young Robert F. Kennedy briefly worked as an assistant counsel for a Senate subcommittee chaired by this man, whose chief counsel was Roy Cohn. This man had become chairman of that Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations in 1953, after Republicans won control of the Senate.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this senator from Wisconsin who led a hunt for suspected communists in the early 1950s.

tossups.p: This man demanded to know “Who promoted Peress?” after Irving Peress, an Army dentist accused of communist ties, received a routine promotion and an honorable discharge. This man also investigated the Army Signal Corps laboratories at Fort Monmouth, New Jersey.
tossups.r: Those clashes led to televised hearings about the Army in 1954. For 10 points, name this Wisconsin senator.

tossups.p: In 1953, this man’s aides Roy Cohn and G. David Schine toured Europe looking for “subversive” books in American government libraries overseas. That same year, this man held hearings investigating the Voice of America radio service.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Wisconsin senator who gave his name to an era of anticommunist accusations.

tossups.p: When this man died in 1957 at age 48, Democrat William Proxmire won a special election to fill his Senate seat. Three years earlier, his fellow senators had voted to condemn his conduct.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Wisconsin Republican who led the Second Red Scare’s hunt for communists in government.

tossups.p: In a Lincoln Day speech to a Republican women’s club in February 1950, this man claimed to have a list of 205 people in the State Department who were members of the Communist Party. He later gave smaller numbers, such as 57.
tossups.r: That speech was given in Wheeling, West Virginia. For 10 points, name this Republican senator from Wisconsin.

tossups.p: Arthur Miller’s play _The Crucible_, set during the Salem witch trials, is often read as an allegory for the anticommunist investigations of this man’s era. Miller himself was later questioned by a House committee, not by this senator.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Wisconsin senator whose name became a term for making accusations of disloyalty without proof.

Leading figure of the Second Red Scare in the early 1950s
His name became a word for accusing people of disloyalty without good evidence
Wheeling, West Virginia (February 1950): claimed to have a list of 205 communists in the State Department

The Senate condemned (censured) him in December 1954 by a vote of 67 to 22

Millard Tydings’s subcommittee called his charges “a fraud and a hoax”; Tydings lost reelection in 1950

A former Wisconsin circuit judge who served in the Marine Corps in World War II

Cartoonist Herblock (Herbert Block) is often credited with coining the word for his tactics in a 1950 _Washington Post_ cartoon
