trap.title: Senator, not HUAC
trap.body: Joseph McCarthy was a senator, so he never served on the House Un-American Activities Committee (HUAC), which held the 1947 Hollywood hearings (the “Hollywood Ten”) and the Alger Hiss case that made Richard Nixon famous. Some tossups about the whole era want “McCarthyism” or the “Red Scare,” not the man. Eugene McCarthy, a Minnesota senator who ran for president in 1968, is a different person.
trap.fix: Hollywood blacklists, the Hollywood Ten, and Alger Hiss point to HUAC. Wheeling, the 1954 Army hearings, Joseph Welch, Edward R. Murrow, and the 1954 censure point to Joseph McCarthy. Listen for “this senator” versus “this committee,” “this era,” or “this term.”
trap.line: Real answer line: Joseph McCarthy (accept Joe McCarthy; do not accept “Eugene McCarthy”)

topics.name: Mayflower
topics.kicker: Ship that carried the Pilgrims to America · Sailed from England in 1620
topics.briefing: In September 1620, a cramped merchant ship called the _Mayflower_ left Plymouth, England, with about 102 passengers, after its leaky partner ship, the _Speedwell_, had to turn back. After about two months at sea, the Pilgrims reached Cape Cod, where 41 men signed the Mayflower Compact before they settled at Plymouth. About half of them died that first winter, but millions of Americans descend from the survivors.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: When a main beam cracked during a storm on this ship’s most famous voyage, passengers used a “great iron screw” they had brought from Holland to raise it back into place. This ship’s master was Christopher Jones.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this ship that carried the Pilgrims from England to America in 1620.

tossups.p: During a storm, a young servant named John Howland fell overboard from this ship but survived by grabbing a trailing rope until sailors hauled him back aboard. A baby named Oceanus Hopkins was born on this ship while it was at sea.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this ship that carried the Pilgrims across the Atlantic in 1620.

tossups.p: This ship and its partner, the _Speedwell_, set out from Southampton in 1620, but they had to turn back twice because the _Speedwell_ leaked. This ship finally crossed the Atlantic alone, leaving England in September.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this ship that brought the Pilgrims to the New World, where they founded Plymouth Colony.

tossups.p: Peregrine White, the first English child born in New England, was born aboard this ship in November 1620 while it lay at anchor off present-day Provincetown. His mother, Susanna, was widowed that winter and then married Edward Winslow in the colony’s first wedding.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this ship whose passengers went on to found Plymouth Colony in Massachusetts.

tossups.p: Passenger Stephen Hopkins had survived the wreck of the _Sea Venture_ on Bermuda in 1609 and spent time at Jamestown before returning to England. Myles Standish and William Brewster were also passengers on this ship.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this ship that carried the Pilgrims across the Atlantic to Massachusetts in 1620.

tossups.p: This ship’s passengers held a patent from the Virginia Company to settle near the mouth of the Hudson River, but dangerous shoals forced the ship to turn back north. Because they would be settling outside that company’s territory, some passengers claimed no one had authority over them.
tossups.r: In response, 41 men signed a compact aboard this ship in November 1620. For 10 points, name this Pilgrim ship.

tossups.p: John Alden, a barrel maker hired for this ship’s voyage, is a main character in Henry Wadsworth Longfellow’s poem _The Courtship of Miles Standish_, in which Priscilla Mullins asks, “Why don’t you speak for yourself, John?”
tossups.r: Alden and Mullins later married. For 10 points, name this ship that carried the Pilgrims to America in 1620.

tossups.p: This ship sailed home to England in April 1621, after many of its sailors had died during a harsh winter in New England. Its master died the next year, and by 1624 the ship was described as lying in ruins.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this ship that had carried the Pilgrims to America in 1620.

tossups.p: Many of this ship’s passengers were Separatists who had spent about a decade living in Leiden, in the Netherlands, while others, sometimes called “Strangers,” were recruited by the London investors who paid for the voyage.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this ship whose passengers, known as the Pilgrims, sailed to America in 1620.

tossups.p: A full-size copy of this ship was built in Brixham, England, and sailed across the Atlantic in 1957 as a gift from Britain to the United States. That copy was restored in time for the 400th anniversary of the original ship’s voyage in 2020.
tossups.r: The original ship carried the Pilgrims to Massachusetts in 1620. For 10 points, name this ship.

tossups.p: William Bradford’s history of his colony describes a proud young sailor on this ship who cursed the seasick passengers, then fell ill and died before the voyage ended. This ship’s crossing of the Atlantic took 66 days.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this ship that carried the Pilgrims to America in 1620.

tossups.p: During the first winter, many of this ship’s passengers kept living aboard while houses were built on shore, and about half of them died of disease before spring. John Carver, who had been chosen governor aboard this ship, died in April 1621.
tossups.r: William Bradford then became governor. For 10 points, name this ship that carried the Pilgrims to Plymouth in 1620.

tossups.p: A granite tower in Provincetown, completed in 1910, honors the spot where this ship first anchored in New England. Its passengers spent about a month exploring the coast before choosing a harbor across the bay for their settlement.
tossups.r: They named that settlement Plymouth. For 10 points, name this ship that carried the Pilgrims in 1620.

tossups.p: This ship’s master and part-owner, Christopher Jones, came from the English port of Harwich and was buried at Rotherhithe, on the River Thames, in 1622. Before 1620, this merchant ship often carried wine from France to England.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this ship that carried the Pilgrims across the Atlantic in 1620.

tossups.p: William Butten, a young servant, was the only passenger who died during this ship’s crossing, just days before land was sighted. About 102 passengers had been crowded below its decks for the voyage.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this ship whose passengers signed a compact before founding Plymouth Colony in 1620.

clues.t: Ship that carried the Pilgrims from England to America in 1620
Its passengers founded Plymouth Colony in Massachusetts
41 men signed a compact aboard it in November 1620 to form a government
Reached Cape Cod in November 1620, after about two months at sea
Its leaky partner ship, the _Speedwell_, turned back twice, so it crossed alone from Plymouth, England, in September 1620
Its master was Christopher Jones
Carried about 102 passengers; many were Separatists who had lived in Leiden, in the Netherlands
Peregrine White, the first English child born in New England, was born aboard while it was anchored off Cape Cod
Oceanus Hopkins was born on board during the voyage, at sea
About half of its passengers died during the first winter (1620–1621), many while still living aboard
Passenger William Bradford became governor and wrote the history _Of Plymouth Plantation_
Passengers included John Carver (the first governor), Myles Standish (military leader), and William Brewster (religious elder)
A cracked main beam was raised back into place with a “great iron screw” brought from Holland
John Howland fell overboard in a storm and survived by grabbing a trailing rope
Stephen Hopkins had survived the _Sea Venture_ wreck on Bermuda (1609) and spent time in Jamestown
Its passengers’ patent from the Virginia Company was for land near the Hudson River; shoals turned the ship back north
Barrel maker John Alden married Priscilla Mullins; in Longfellow’s _The Courtship of Miles Standish_ she asks, “Why don’t you speak for yourself, John?”
Sailed home in April 1621; Christopher Jones died in 1622, and by 1624 the ship lay in ruins
First anchored off present-day Provincetown; a granite tower, the Pilgrim Monument (1910), honors the spot
The crossing took 66 days; servant William Butten was the only passenger who died at sea
A full-size replica was built in Brixham, England, and sailed to Massachusetts in 1957
A merchant ship that often carried wine; Christopher Jones came from Harwich and was buried at Rotherhithe
“Strangers” (passengers who were not Separatists) were recruited by the London investors who paid for the voyage
Bradford wrote of a proud young sailor who cursed the seasick passengers, then died before the voyage ended

trap.title: Ship, compact, or colony?
trap.body: Three answer lines share the same clues. The _Mayflower_ is the ship; the Mayflower Compact is the agreement 41 men signed aboard it in November 1620; and Plymouth Colony is the settlement they founded. Jamestown (1607, Virginia) was the earlier English colony, and its colonists came on three different ships: the _Susan Constant_, the _Godspeed_, and the _Discovery_.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun: “this ship” or “this vessel” wants the Mayflower; “this document” or “this agreement” wants the Mayflower Compact; “this colony” or “this settlement” wants Plymouth Colony. Answer with exactly what the question asks for.
trap.line: Real answer line: Mayflower (do not accept “Mayflower Compact,” “Plymouth Colony,” or “Speedwell”)

topics.name: Mississippi River
topics.kicker: Great river of the American heartland · Route of explorers and steamboats
topics.briefing: The Mississippi River starts as a stream so small that visitors can cross it on stepping stones at Lake Itasca in Minnesota, then flows more than 2,300 miles south to the Gulf of Mexico. Explorers like Marquette, Jolliet, and La Salle paddled it, steamboats and Mark Twain made it famous, and in the Civil War the Union fought to control it so it could split the Confederacy in two.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Henry Schoolcraft named the lake at this river’s source by joining pieces of the Latin words for “true head.” Where this river flows out of that lake in northern Minnesota, visitors can walk across it on a line of stepping stones.
tossups.r: That lake is Lake Itasca [“eye-TASS-kuh”]. For 10 points, name this river that flows past St. Louis and empties into the Gulf of Mexico below New Orleans.

tossups.p: In 1673, the Jesuit priest Jacques Marquette and the explorer Louis Jolliet paddled down the Wisconsin River into this river, then followed it south as far as the mouth of the Arkansas River. They turned back because they feared meeting the Spanish farther south.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this river that flows past Memphis and New Orleans on its way to the Gulf of Mexico.

tossups.p: In 1682, René-Robert Cavelier, Sieur de La Salle [“luh SAL”], traveled by canoe to the mouth of this river and claimed all the land it drained for France. He named that huge region Louisiana in honor of King Louis XIV.
tossups.r: About a century later, the Treaty of Paris made this river the western border of the United States. For 10 points, name this river that flows past New Orleans.

tossups.p: In 1541, the Spanish explorer Hernando de Soto led the first European expedition known to cross this river. When de Soto died of a fever the next year, his men sank his body in this river so that the Native peoples nearby would not learn he was dead.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this river that flows past Memphis on its way to the Gulf of Mexico.

tossups.p: Pinckney’s Treaty of 1795 gave Americans the right to ship goods down this river and store them at a port near its mouth without paying duties. When Spanish officials took away that “right of deposit” in 1802, Thomas Jefferson sent James Monroe to France to try to buy that port.
tossups.r: The Louisiana Purchase soon gave the United States a huge area of land west of this river. For 10 points, name this river that flows past New Orleans.

tossups.p: The New Madrid [“MAD-rid”] earthquakes of 1811 and 1812 were so strong that witnesses said they made this river flow backward for a short time, and they created Reelfoot Lake in Tennessee. That winter, the _New Orleans_ became the first steamboat to travel down this river.
tossups.r: Mark Twain later worked as a steamboat pilot on this river. For 10 points, name this river that flows past St. Louis and Memphis.

tossups.p: In the late 1850s, a river pilot named Horace Bixby taught one young man to steer steamboats on this river. That man took his pen name from a crew member’s call meaning the water was two fathoms, or twelve feet, deep.
tossups.r: That writer described his piloting days in a memoir about “life on” this river. For 10 points, name this river that flows past Mark Twain’s boyhood home of Hannibal, Missouri.

tossups.p: In one novel, a boy and a man who has escaped slavery plan to reach Cairo [“KAY-roh”], Illinois, so they can travel up the Ohio River into the free states, but they drift past it in a thick fog. Earlier, the two had met while hiding on Jackson’s Island.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this river that Huckleberry Finn and Jim travel down on a raft in a Mark Twain novel.

tossups.p: After Union victories at Vicksburg and Port Hudson in 1863, Abraham Lincoln wrote that “the Father of Waters again goes unvexed to the sea.” Winfield Scott’s Anaconda Plan had called for the Union to blockade Southern ports and take control of this river, cutting the Confederacy in two.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this river that the Union took control of to split the Confederacy, which flows past Memphis and New Orleans.

tossups.p: Secretary of Commerce Herbert Hoover directed relief efforts during this river’s Great Flood of 1927, which drove hundreds of thousands of people from their homes. The next year, Congress put the Army Corps of Engineers in charge of controlling floods along this river.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this river that flows from Minnesota past St. Louis and Memphis to the Gulf of Mexico.

tossups.p: James Eads designed a steel arch bridge across this river at St. Louis that opened in 1874, and Andrew Carnegie’s Keystone Bridge Company built it. Nearly a century later, Eero Saarinen’s [“AIR-oh SAR-uh-nen”] Gateway Arch was completed on this river’s bank in the same city.
tossups.r: The Missouri River joins this river just north of that city. For 10 points, name this river that flows south to New Orleans.

tossups.p: Monks Mound, the largest earthwork built in the Americas before Columbus arrived, stands at Cahokia [“kuh-HOH-kee-uh”], a city that flourished about a thousand years ago near this river, across from present-day St. Louis. This river’s name comes from an Ojibwe [“oh-JIB-way”] word meaning “great river.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this river that flows from Minnesota to the Gulf of Mexico.

tossups.p: The Army Corps of Engineers built the Old River Control Structure to stop this river from shifting most of its flow into the shorter Atchafalaya [“uh-CHAF-uh-LY-uh”] River. Mud carried by this river has built a “bird’s-foot” delta that sticks out into the sea southeast of New Orleans.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this river that carries barges past Baton Rouge and New Orleans.

tossups.p: In April 1865, the overcrowded steamboat _Sultana_ exploded on this river near Memphis in the deadliest ship disaster in U.S. history; most of the people who died were Union soldiers going home from Confederate prison camps at the end of the Civil War.
tossups.r: In the musical _Show Boat_, the song “Ol’ Man River” is about this river. For 10 points, name this river where Mark Twain once piloted steamboats.

tossups.p: Father Louis Hennepin named the only major natural waterfall on this river after Saint Anthony of Padua, and that waterfall later powered the flour mills of Minneapolis. Far downstream, the Ohio River joins this river at Cairo [“KAY-roh”], Illinois.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this river that begins at Lake Itasca and ends at the Gulf of Mexico.

clues.t: Flows south from Minnesota into the Gulf of Mexico, which a 2025 executive order renamed the “Gulf of America” for U.S. government use
Flows past Minneapolis, St. Louis, Memphis, Baton Rouge, and New Orleans
Huckleberry Finn and Jim float down it on a raft in Mark Twain’s novel
Mark Twain grew up beside it in Hannibal, Missouri, and later piloted steamboats on it
Begins at Lake Itasca in northern Minnesota, where visitors can cross it on stepping stones
The Missouri River joins it just north of St. Louis, and the Ohio River joins it at Cairo, Illinois
Jacques Marquette and Louis Jolliet paddled down it in 1673, turning back at the mouth of the Arkansas River
La Salle reached its mouth in 1682 and claimed all the land it drained for France, naming it Louisiana after Louis XIV
Hernando de Soto’s Spanish expedition crossed it in 1541; when he died the next year, his men sank his body in it
The Anaconda Plan aimed to control it; Ulysses S. Grant’s capture of Vicksburg (July 4, 1863) split the Confederacy in two
The Louisiana Purchase (1803) gave the United States New Orleans and a huge area of land west of it
The Treaty of Paris (1783) made it the western border of the United States
Its name comes from an Ojibwe word meaning “great river”
Henry Schoolcraft identified its source in 1832 and made up the name Itasca from the Latin words “veritas caput” (“true head”)
Pinckney’s Treaty (1795) let Americans ship goods down it and store them at New Orleans (the “right of deposit”)
The New Madrid earthquakes (1811–1812) reportedly made it flow backward for a short time and created Reelfoot Lake in Tennessee
The _New Orleans_ became the first steamboat to travel down it (1811–1812), on a voyage led by Nicholas Roosevelt
Twain learned piloting from Horace Bixby and wrote an 1883 memoir about his “life on” it; his pen name was a call meaning two fathoms (12 feet) deep
Huck and Jim meet on Jackson’s Island and plan to head up the Ohio River from Cairo, Illinois, but miss Cairo in a fog
After Vicksburg and Port Hudson fell (1863), Lincoln wrote: “The Father of Waters again goes unvexed to the sea”
The steamboat _Sultana_ exploded on it near Memphis in April 1865, the deadliest ship disaster in U.S. history
James Eads’s steel arch bridge at St. Louis opened in 1874; Eero Saarinen’s Gateway Arch was finished on its bank in 1965
Great Flood of 1927: Herbert Hoover led the relief effort, and the Flood Control Act of 1928 put the Army Corps of Engineers in charge of its levees
The Old River Control Structure keeps it from shifting into the Atchafalaya River; its mouth is a “bird’s-foot” delta
Mound builders built the city of Cahokia near it, across from St. Louis; Monks Mound there is the largest earthwork built in the Americas before Columbus
The song “Ol’ Man River,” from Jerome Kern and Oscar Hammerstein II’s musical _Show Boat_ (1927), is about it
Father Louis Hennepin named Saint Anthony Falls (1680), its only major natural waterfall, which later powered the flour mills of Minneapolis

trap.title: Mississippi or Missouri?
trap.body: The Missouri River is the Mississippi’s longest tributary, and the two meet just north of St. Louis, so river clues from that area can fit either one. Civil War clues are another trap: the Anaconda Plan and the Siege of Vicksburg have their own answer lines, so if a question asks for “this plan” or “this siege,” naming the river is wrong. A question about “this state” wants the state of Mississippi instead.
trap.fix: Lake Itasca, de Soto, Marquette and Jolliet, La Salle, Mark Twain, New Orleans, and the Gulf of Mexico mean the Mississippi; Lewis and Clark, the Great Plains, and Montana mean the Missouri. Listen for the noun before you buzz, then just say “Mississippi.”
trap.line: Real answer line: Mississippi River (do not accept “Missouri River”)

topics.name: Missouri Compromise
topics.kicker: 1820 deal on where slavery could spread · Drew the 36°30′ line
topics.briefing: Thomas Jefferson said the fight over Missouri woke him “like a fire bell in the night.” By late 1819 the Union had 11 free states and 11 slave states, so Missouri’s request to join as a slave state threatened the balance in the Senate. The 1820 deal let Missouri in with slavery, added Maine as a free state, and banned slavery in the rest of the Louisiana Purchase north of the 36°30′ line, a rule that lasted until the Kansas–Nebraska Act of 1854.
topics.answerHtml: Missouri Compromise (accept Compromise of 1820; prompt on “Missouri” or “compromise” alone; do not accept “Compromise of 1850”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Senator Jesse Thomas of Illinois added a provision to this agreement that banned slavery in the rest of the Louisiana Purchase north of 36 degrees, 30 minutes north latitude. Speaker of the House Henry Clay helped push this deal through Congress.
tossups.r: It admitted Maine to the Union as a free state. For 10 points, name this 1820 agreement over the spread of slavery.

tossups.p: New York congressman James Tallmadge set off the fight that led to this agreement by proposing that slavery be ended gradually in a territory that wanted to become a state. His amendment passed the House, where free states had more members, but it failed in the Senate.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1820 deal that admitted Maine as a free state and drew a line across the Louisiana Purchase.

tossups.p: In an 1820 letter about the fight over this agreement, Thomas Jefferson compared slavery to holding “the wolf by the ear.” In the same letter, he said that fight had woken him “like a fire bell in the night.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1820 agreement that banned slavery north of a line at 36 degrees, 30 minutes north latitude in the Louisiana Purchase.

tossups.p: John Quincy Adams wrote in his diary that the debate over this agreement was “a title-page to a great tragic volume.” During that debate, Senator Rufus King of New York was a leading opponent of admitting another slave state.
tossups.r: This deal also let Maine become a state separate from Massachusetts. For 10 points, name this 1820 agreement.

tossups.p: Kentucky senator John Crittenden tried to prevent the Civil War by proposing to bring back this agreement’s dividing line and extend it west to the Pacific Ocean. That line ran along 36 degrees, 30 minutes north latitude.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1820 agreement, pushed through Congress with help from Henry Clay, that admitted Maine as a free state.

tossups.p: A year after this agreement passed, Henry Clay worked out a second deal because the constitution written for a new slave state tried to keep free Black people from moving there. That state finally entered the Union in 1821 as the 24th state.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1820 agreement that paired the admission of that slave state with the admission of Maine as a free state.

tossups.p: Dred Scott argued that he had become free while living at Fort Snelling, in a territory where this agreement banned slavery. In 1857, Chief Justice Roger Taney [“TAW-nee”] ruled that Congress had never had the power to ban slavery in the territories, so this agreement’s ban was unconstitutional.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1820 agreement that drew a line at 36 degrees, 30 minutes north latitude.

tossups.p: The Republican Party was founded in 1854 by people angry about a bill that would end this agreement. That bill, Stephen Douglas’s Kansas–Nebraska Act, let settlers vote on slavery instead, an idea called popular sovereignty.
tossups.r: This agreement had admitted Maine as a free state in 1820. For 10 points, name this agreement associated with Henry Clay.

tossups.p: In an 1854 speech at Peoria, Illinois, Abraham Lincoln attacked the law that had just repealed this agreement. This agreement had banned slavery in the lands of the Louisiana Purchase north of a certain line, except in one new state.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1820 agreement that also admitted Maine as a free state.

tossups.p: William King led the movement that finally separated a northern district from Massachusetts as part of this agreement, and King became the first governor of the new state. This agreement balanced that free state with a new slave state west of the Mississippi River.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1820 agreement, pushed through by Henry Clay, that admitted Maine as the 23rd state.

tossups.p: President James Monroe asked his cabinet whether Congress had the power to ban slavery in the territories before he signed this agreement in March 1820. At the time, the Union had 11 free states and 11 slave states.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this agreement that kept that balance by admitting Maine as a free state along with a new slave state.

tossups.p: The dividing line drawn by this agreement follows most of the border between Arkansas and the state to its north, except for that state’s “Bootheel.” North of that line, this agreement banned slavery in the lands of the Louisiana Purchase.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1820 agreement that paired Maine’s admission as a free state with a new slave state.

tossups.p: John Randolph of Virginia mocked the Northern congressmen who voted with the South during the debate over this agreement as “doughfaces.” After this agreement fully took effect, the Union had 12 free states and 12 slave states.
tossups.r: This agreement admitted Maine as the 23rd state. For 10 points, name this deal that Henry Clay helped pass in 1820.

tossups.p: This was the first of three deals, along with a tariff bargain in 1833 and a group of laws in 1850, that earned Henry Clay his reputation for settling fights between the North and the South. This deal divided the Louisiana Purchase lands into slave and free areas.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1820 agreement that admitted Maine as a free state and drew a line at 36 degrees, 30 minutes.

tossups.p: The northern border of the Texas Panhandle runs along the same line of latitude that this agreement used to divide slave and free land. Violence broke out in “Bleeding Kansas” after Congress repealed this agreement in 1854.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1820 deal that let Maine join the Union as a free state.

clues.t: Admitted Missouri as a slave state and Maine as a free state, keeping the Senate balanced
Passed by Congress in 1820 and signed by President James Monroe
Banned slavery in the rest of the Louisiana Purchase north of 36°30′ north latitude
Henry Clay, “the Great Compromiser,” helped push it through Congress as Speaker of the House
Repealed by Stephen Douglas’s Kansas–Nebraska Act (1854), which let settlers vote on slavery (popular sovereignty) and led to “Bleeding Kansas”
Ruled unconstitutional in _Dred Scott v. Sandford_ (1857) by Chief Justice Roger Taney
Thomas Jefferson said the crisis over it woke him “like a fire bell in the night”
Maine had been part of Massachusetts until it became the 23rd state in 1820
The Tallmadge Amendment (1819), which would have ended slavery in Missouri gradually, set off the crisis; it passed the House but failed in the Senate
Kept the balance: 11 free and 11 slave states before it, and 12 of each after both new states joined
The Republican Party was founded in 1854 by opponents of the bill that repealed it
A second deal (1821), also worked out by Clay, settled a fight over Missouri’s constitution, which tried to bar free Black people; Missouri became the 24th state
Senator Jesse Thomas of Illinois proposed the amendment that drew the 36°30′ line
In the same 1820 letter, to John Holmes, Jefferson said that with slavery “we have the wolf by the ear”
John Quincy Adams called the debate over it “a title-page to a great tragic volume”
Senator Rufus King of New York was a leading opponent of admitting another slave state
John Randolph of Virginia mocked Northern congressmen who voted with the South as “doughfaces”
Monroe asked his cabinet whether Congress could ban slavery in the territories before signing it in March 1820
William King led Maine’s statehood movement and became Maine’s first governor
Dred Scott claimed freedom partly because he had lived at Fort Snelling, in territory where it banned slavery
Abraham Lincoln attacked its repeal in his 1854 Peoria speech
The Crittenden Compromise (1860) tried to avoid war by bringing back its line and extending it west to the Pacific
Its line follows most of Missouri’s southern border with Arkansas (all but the Bootheel) and the Texas Panhandle’s northern border
The first of three sectional deals that Henry Clay helped make, followed by the Compromise Tariff of 1833 and the Compromise of 1850

trap.title: 1820 or 1850?
trap.body: Henry Clay helped pass both the Missouri Compromise (1820) and the Compromise of 1850, and both dealt with slavery in new lands, so an early buzz can go wrong. The Compromise of 1850 admitted California as a free state and added a tougher Fugitive Slave Act, while the Missouri Compromise admitted Maine and Missouri and drew the 36°30′ line. The Kansas–Nebraska Act (1854) is a third answer line: it repealed the Missouri Compromise.
trap.fix: Maine, 36°30′, Jefferson’s “fire bell,” Tallmadge, and James Monroe mean 1820. California, the Fugitive Slave Act, Daniel Webster’s “Seventh of March” speech, Millard Fillmore, and Utah and New Mexico mean 1850. “Compromise of 1820” is fine, but never say “Compromise of 1850” for this answer.
trap.line: Real answer line: Missouri Compromise (accept Compromise of 1820; do not accept “Compromise of 1850”)

topics.name: New Deal
topics.kicker: FDR’s answer to the Great Depression · Relief, recovery, and reform
topics.briefing: When Franklin Roosevelt became president in 1933, about one in four American workers had no job, and thousands of banks had failed. His New Deal answered with a flood of new laws and “alphabet agencies,” such as the CCC, the TVA, and the WPA, that put millions of people to work building roads, dams, schools, and parks. It also created Social Security, which pays pensions to retired workers, and it sparked heated debates, including fights with the Supreme Court.
topics.answerHtml: New Deal (do not accept “Square Deal,” “Fair Deal,” or “Great Society”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In the “sick chicken” case, _Schechter_ [“SHEK-ter”] _Poultry Corp. v. United States_, the Supreme Court unanimously struck down this program’s National Industrial Recovery Act. Businesses that followed that law’s rules had displayed a blue eagle with the motto “We Do Our Part.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this group of programs that Franklin Roosevelt created to fight the Great Depression.

tossups.p: After the Supreme Court struck down several laws from this program, its creator proposed adding up to six new justices in 1937. Justice Owen Roberts’s vote in a 1937 case upholding a minimum-wage law was nicknamed “the switch in time that saved nine.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this set of programs, including the WPA and Social Security, that Franklin Roosevelt used to fight the Great Depression.

tossups.p: Ida May Fuller of Vermont received the first monthly check from a 1935 law that was part of this program. Frances Perkins, the first woman to serve in a presidential cabinet, led the committee that designed that law, the Social Security Act.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this program of Franklin Roosevelt’s, which also created the CCC and the WPA.

tossups.p: Hallie Flanagan led a theater project paid for by this program, and its Federal Writers’ Project hired authors such as Zora Neale Hurston and Richard Wright. Both projects belonged to the Works Progress Administration, which Harry Hopkins ran.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this collection of Franklin Roosevelt’s programs that fought the Great Depression.

tossups.p: Utility company president Wendell Willkie fought a public power agency created by this program, then ran for president against its creator in 1940. That agency, the Tennessee Valley Authority, built dams such as Norris Dam to control floods and make electricity.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this group of 1930s programs that Franklin Roosevelt promised the American people.

tossups.p: Francis Townsend proposed a pension for every American aged 60 or older, and Huey Long called for a “Share Our Wealth” plan, because both men thought this program did not go far enough. From the other side, the American Liberty League argued that this program gave the government too much power.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this set of programs, including Social Security, that Franklin Roosevelt created during the Great Depression.

tossups.p: Dorothea Lange took the photograph _Migrant Mother_ while working for the Resettlement Administration, one of many agencies created by this program. Another of its agencies, the Rural Electrification Administration, brought electric power lines to farms across the country.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this set of 1930s programs that included the Social Security Act.

tossups.p: Advisers such as Raymond Moley and Rexford Tugwell, a group nicknamed the “Brain Trust,” helped plan this program. Its name came from a promise made in 1932 by a candidate who flew to Chicago to accept the Democratic nomination in person.
tossups.r: That candidate was Franklin Roosevelt. Its goals were summed up as “relief, recovery, and reform.” For 10 points, name this program that fought the Great Depression.

tossups.p: In _United States v. Butler_, the Supreme Court struck down a law from this program that paid farmers to grow fewer crops so that prices would rise. Under that law, the Agricultural Adjustment Act, some farmers were even paid to plow under cotton that they had already planted.
tossups.r: It also created the Civilian Conservation Corps. For 10 points, name this group of programs from Franklin Roosevelt’s presidency.

tossups.p: Workers in one agency of this program earned 30 dollars a month and had to send most of that pay home to their families. Those young men planted billions of trees and built trails and cabins in parks for the Civilian Conservation Corps.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this group of programs Franklin Roosevelt used to fight the Great Depression.

tossups.p: The Fair Labor Standards Act, which set the first national minimum wage in 1938, was one of the last major laws of this program. Three years earlier, its Wagner Act had protected workers’ right to form unions and created the National Labor Relations Board.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this set of programs that Franklin Roosevelt created during the Great Depression.

tossups.p: Interior Secretary Harold Ickes [“ICK-eez”] ran this program’s Public Works Administration, which paid private companies to build bridges, dams, and schools. Harry Hopkins ran several of its relief agencies, including the Civil Works Administration, which hired millions of people during the winter of 1933 to 1934.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this group of programs, including the WPA, that Franklin Roosevelt began in 1933.

tossups.p: Before he was elected to Congress, a young Lyndon Johnson ran this program’s National Youth Administration in Texas, which gave part-time jobs to students and other young people. Laws for this program were passed in two big waves, in 1933 and 1935.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this program whose “alphabet agencies” included the NYA, the CCC, and the TVA.

tossups.p: Joseph Kennedy became the first chairman of the Securities and Exchange Commission, which this program created to police the stock market. The Glass-Steagall Act, another part of this program, created the FDIC to insure people’s bank deposits.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this program that Franklin Roosevelt promised the American people in 1932.

tossups.p: This program began with a national “bank holiday” and the Emergency Banking Act, which Congress passed in a single day in March 1933. Congress passed so many of this program’s laws over the next few months that the period became known as the Hundred Days.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this group of programs Franklin Roosevelt created to fight the Great Depression.

clues.t: Franklin D. Roosevelt’s programs to fight the Great Depression (1933–1939)
Its goals are summed up as the “three R’s”: relief, recovery, and reform
Created “alphabet agencies” known by their initials, like the CCC, the TVA, and the WPA
Included the Social Security Act (1935), which created pensions for retired workers and unemployment insurance
FDR first promised it in 1932, when he flew to Chicago to accept the Democratic nomination in person
Began in the “Hundred Days” of 1933 with a “bank holiday” and the Emergency Banking Act
Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC): young men planted billions of trees and built trails and cabins in parks
Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA, 1933): built dams to control floods and bring electricity to the region
Works Progress Administration (WPA, 1935), led by Harry Hopkins, hired millions of people to build roads, bridges, and schools
Labor Secretary Frances Perkins, the first woman in a presidential cabinet, led the committee that designed Social Security
After the Supreme Court struck down some of its laws, FDR proposed adding up to six justices (the 1937 “court-packing” plan)
The Wagner Act (1935) protected workers’ right to form unions and created the National Labor Relations Board
The FDIC (1933) insures bank deposits, and the SEC (1934) polices the stock market
_Schechter Poultry Corp. v. United States_ (1935), the “sick chicken” case, struck down the National Industrial Recovery Act; the NRA’s symbol was a blue eagle
_United States v. Butler_ (1936) struck down the Agricultural Adjustment Act, which paid farmers to grow less
Owen Roberts’s vote in _West Coast Hotel Co. v. Parrish_ (1937), upholding a minimum-wage law, was called “the switch in time that saved nine”
Huey Long (“Share Our Wealth”) and Francis Townsend said it did too little; the American Liberty League said it gave the government too much power
The Fair Labor Standards Act (1938), one of its last major laws, set the first national minimum wage and limited child labor
Ida May Fuller of Vermont received the first monthly Social Security check (1940)
WPA arts projects hired writers like Zora Neale Hurston and Richard Wright; Hallie Flanagan led the Federal Theatre Project
Dorothea Lange took the photograph _Migrant Mother_ (1936) for its Resettlement Administration
The Rural Electrification Administration (1935) brought electric power lines to farms
Advisers called the “Brain Trust,” including Raymond Moley and Rexford Tugwell, helped plan it
A young Lyndon Johnson ran the National Youth Administration in Texas, which gave part-time jobs to students
Utility executive Wendell Willkie fought the TVA, then ran against FDR as the Republican nominee in 1940
Harold Ickes ran the Public Works Administration; Harry Hopkins’s Civil Works Administration hired millions in the winter of 1933–1934
Joseph Kennedy, father of a future president, was the first chairman of the Securities and Exchange Commission

trap.title: Which deal is it?
trap.body: Presidents love catchy names for their programs, and quiz bowl loves to mix them up: Theodore Roosevelt’s Square Deal, Franklin Roosevelt’s New Deal, Harry Truman’s Fair Deal, and Lyndon Johnson’s Great Society. Another trap is answering “Great Depression,” which was the crisis, not the programs created to fight it.
trap.fix: Match the president and the decade. The 1930s, FDR, alphabet agencies, Social Security, and fights with the Supreme Court mean the New Deal. The “three Cs” of conservation, control of corporations, and consumer protection mean the Square Deal; Truman’s plan for national health insurance means the Fair Deal; Medicare and the War on Poverty mean the Great Society.
trap.line: Real answer line: New Deal (do not accept “Square Deal,” “Fair Deal,” or “Great Society”)

topics.name: Philadelphia
topics.kicker: William Penn’s Quaker city · Where the Declaration and Constitution were signed
topics.briefing: William Penn, a Quaker, founded Philadelphia in 1682 and gave it a Greek name meaning “brotherly love.” By the 1770s it was the largest city in the colonies, and its State House, later renamed Independence Hall, saw the signing of both the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution. It served as the nation’s capital from 1790 to 1800 and is home to the cracked Liberty Bell.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Surveyor Thomas Holme helped plan this city on a grid of straight streets between the Delaware and Schuylkill [“SKOO-kul”] rivers, with five public squares, one at its center and one in each quarter. Its City Hall was later built on the central square.
tossups.r: Its Quaker founder, William Penn, gave it a name meaning “brotherly love.” For 10 points, name this largest city in Pennsylvania.

tossups.p: In 1796, Ona Judge escaped from slavery at the President’s House in this city, where George Washington lived while he was president. Washington and John Adams both lived in this city because it served as the national capital from 1790 to 1800.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this city where the Constitution was written, the largest city in Pennsylvania.

tossups.p: On July 8, 1776, Colonel John Nixon read a document that had just been approved by Congress to a crowd in the yard behind this city’s State House. Eleven years later, delegates met inside that State House to write a new plan of government.
tossups.r: That building is Independence Hall. For 10 points, name this city where the Declaration of Independence was signed.

tossups.p: Abolitionist William Still recorded the stories of hundreds of freedom seekers who passed through this city on the Underground Railroad, including groups guided by Harriet Tubman. Earlier, the first antislavery society in America was founded in this city in 1775.
tossups.r: Its Quaker founder was William Penn. For 10 points, name this Pennsylvania city where the Liberty Bell is displayed.

tossups.p: Richard Allen founded Mother Bethel Church in this city, and in 1816 he became the first bishop of the African Methodist Episcopal Church, which was organized there. Years earlier, Allen and Absalom Jones had started the Free African Society in this city.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this city where the Second Continental Congress met, the largest city in Pennsylvania.

tossups.p: Al Capone was once held at this city’s Eastern State Penitentiary, a prison built in 1829 that kept inmates alone in their cells so they would reflect on their crimes. ENIAC, one of the first electronic computers, was unveiled at a university in this city in 1946.
tossups.r: This city is also home to the Liberty Bell. For 10 points, name this city where the Declaration of Independence was signed.

tossups.p: After the British left this city in 1778, Benedict Arnold became its military commander and married Peggy Shippen, a young woman from a wealthy family there. The British had captured this city in 1777, forcing Congress to flee west to Lancaster and then York.
tossups.r: While the British held it, Washington’s army camped at nearby Valley Forge. For 10 points, name this city, the U.S. capital during most of the 1790s.

tossups.p: During a yellow fever epidemic in 1793, Dr. Benjamin Rush treated patients in this city by bloodletting, and Richard Allen and Absalom Jones organized Black volunteers to nurse the sick. That epidemic killed thousands of people and drove the federal government out of this city for a time.
tossups.r: It was the U.S. capital at the time. For 10 points, name this Pennsylvania city where Benjamin Franklin lived.

tossups.p: Alexander Graham Bell showed off his new telephone at this city’s Centennial Exposition of 1876, where visitors could also see the torch-holding arm of the Statue of Liberty. That world’s fair was held in this city’s huge Fairmount Park.
tossups.r: It marked 100 years since the Declaration of Independence was signed here. For 10 points, name this Pennsylvania city.

tossups.p: This city’s Library Company, founded in 1731, and its Union Fire Company, founded in 1736, were both started by a printer who had arrived there as a 17-year-old runaway from Boston. That printer is buried in this city’s Christ Church Burial Ground.
tossups.r: That printer was Benjamin Franklin. For 10 points, name this city where Franklin signed both the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution.

tossups.p: For most of the 1900s, an unwritten agreement kept every building in this city lower than the hat on the statue of its founder atop City Hall. One Liberty Place finally broke that rule when it was finished in 1987.
tossups.r: That founder, William Penn, was a Quaker. For 10 points, name this largest city in Pennsylvania.

tossups.p: Abolitionists gave a famous object in this city its nickname, inspired by its inscription from the Book of Leviticus: “Proclaim LIBERTY throughout all the Land unto all the Inhabitants thereof.” That bell cracked soon after it arrived, was recast, and later cracked again.
tossups.r: It is displayed near Independence Hall. For 10 points, name this city, home of the Liberty Bell.

tossups.p: Delegates from twelve colonies met at this city’s Carpenters’ Hall in 1774, partly in response to the Intolerable Acts. Years later, the First Bank of the United States, which Alexander Hamilton had proposed, was built nearby.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this city where the First Continental Congress met, the U.S. capital from 1790 to 1800.

tossups.p: George Washington’s Farewell Address first appeared in 1796 in a newspaper published in this city, where Washington lived as president. In a famous movie scene, the boxer Rocky Balboa trains by running up the steps of this city’s art museum.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Pennsylvania city, home of the Liberty Bell and Independence Hall.

tossups.p: David Rittenhouse, an astronomer who became the first director of the U.S. Mint, has one of this city’s original public squares named for him. The Mint opened in this city in 1792, while it was the nation’s capital.
tossups.r: Legend says Betsy Ross sewed the first American flag here. For 10 points, name this city founded by William Penn.

clues.t: Founded in 1682 by the Quaker William Penn as the capital of his colony of Pennsylvania
Its name comes from Greek words meaning “brotherly love”
The Declaration of Independence (1776) and the Constitution (1787) were both signed at its Independence Hall
Home of the cracked Liberty Bell
U.S. capital from 1790 to 1800, before the government moved to Washington, D.C.
The First Continental Congress met at its Carpenters’ Hall (1774); the Second met at its State House
Benjamin Franklin’s adopted home: he ran away there from Boston at 17 and is buried there
Legend says Betsy Ross sewed the first American flag in her house there
Lies where the Schuylkill River meets the Delaware River
The British captured it in 1777 after the Battle of Brandywine; Washington lost at Germantown and then camped at nearby Valley Forge
Hosted the 1876 Centennial Exposition, where Alexander Graham Bell showed off the telephone
A yellow fever epidemic in 1793 killed thousands and drove the federal government out for a time
In the movie _Rocky_ (1976), the boxer Rocky Balboa runs up the steps of its art museum
Surveyor Thomas Holme helped lay it out on a grid with five public squares; City Hall stands on the central one
Colonel John Nixon read the Declaration aloud to a crowd in the State House Yard on July 8, 1776
Ona Judge escaped from slavery at the President’s House there in 1796, while George Washington lived there
Richard Allen founded Mother Bethel Church; the African Methodist Episcopal (AME) Church was organized there in 1816
William Still recorded the stories of hundreds of freedom seekers passing through on the Underground Railroad
The first American antislavery society was founded there in 1775; Benjamin Franklin later became its president
Benedict Arnold was its military commander in 1778 and married Peggy Shippen there
Eastern State Penitentiary (1829) kept prisoners alone in their cells; Al Capone was once held there
ENIAC, one of the first electronic computers, was unveiled at the University of Pennsylvania there in 1946
Franklin founded its Library Company (1731) and Union Fire Company (1736) and is buried in its Christ Church Burial Ground
By an unwritten agreement, no building rose above the William Penn statue on City Hall until One Liberty Place (1987)
The Liberty Bell’s inscription comes from the Book of Leviticus; abolitionists gave the bell its name
George Washington’s Farewell Address first appeared in one of its newspapers (1796)
The U.S. Mint opened there in 1792; its first director, the astronomer David Rittenhouse, is honored by Rittenhouse Square

trap.title: City, not state
trap.body: Philadelphia and Pennsylvania were both founded by William Penn, so clues about Penn, the Quakers, and the “Holy Experiment” can point to either answer line. If a question asks for “this city,” answering “Pennsylvania” is wrong, and if it asks for “this colony” or “this state,” Philadelphia is wrong. Nearby places such as Valley Forge and Brandywine have their own answers, too.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun. “This city” with Independence Hall, the Liberty Bell, the Continental Congress, or the 1790s capital means Philadelphia. “This colony” or “this state” with Harrisburg, Pittsburgh, Gettysburg, or the Walking Purchase means Pennsylvania.
